For cyclicals, you look at where you are in the cycle, normalized/mid-cycle earnings, price-to-book, capacity, inventory, spreads, not a growth multiple that flatters the peak and punishes the trough. text:
Very bad advice: PEG is a tool for steady compounders. For cyclicals, you look at where you are in the cycle—normalized/mid-cycle earnings, price-to-book, capacity, inventory, spreads—not a growth multiple that flatters the peak and punishes the trough. Using PEG on a cyclical is like judging a rollercoaster by its average height: technically true, practically useless.  PEG doesn't work for cyclicals because it assumes earnings growth is smooth and predictable—cyclical earnings are neither.
 
Here's the simple version:
• PEG = P/E ÷ growth rate. It's designed for companies whose earnings grow steadily year after year (like software or consumer staples). A low PEG is supposed to mean "cheap growth."
• Cyclical earnings swing wildly—autos, steel, airlines, semis, energy. In a boom, earnings spike and the P/E looks low. In a bust, earnings collapse and the P/E looks high (or goes negative).
• So PEG gets it backwards. At the top of the cycle, when the stock is actually most dangerous, trailing growth looks great and PEG looks cheap. At the bottom, when the stock may be cheapest, earnings are troughing, growth looks terrible, and PEG looks expensive—or meaningless.
• The "G" is unreliable. A cyclical's growth rate over the past few years tells you almost nothing about the next few, because it's driven by the cycle, not by a durable compounding engine. You're dividing by a number that's about to reverse.

text:

Telecom CapEx intensity eventually fell below where it started but $AMZN, $GOOGL, $META and $MSFT went from spending ~12% of revenue before AI to a projected 24% by 2030 (even after 2027 peak that's effectively twice old baseline).

I see this one making the rounds as some bearish takedown of AI and in particular neoclouds.

FSD v15 is starting to hit cars today, and I think this is a really BIG one.

A core piece of how the car, the robotaxi and the robot understand the world is now shared.

Then there’s Tesla Reality View.

The familiar gray driving display is now being replaced by a detailed view of the world around the car, created live from a virtual viewpoint above it. Ashok says the same model that drives the car also draws that scene. Arrows show the turns FSD plans to make, and pins show where it wants to park. 

Elon says you can tap a point in that view to tell the car where to go, with turn markers floating overhead like a video game.

$MU $SNDK $SKHY Fair question, and the honest answer is: plenty, starting with this industry.

Micron itself, 2018. At the peak it traded at roughly 4 to 5x forward earnings, with gross margin at a filed 61% in Q4 of fiscal 2018, and the stock still lost about half into 2019 as earnings collapsed. ZIM, 2021 to 2022: near 1 to 2x peak earnings, enormous dividends paid out in cash, and still down roughly 80% from the peak when container rates normalized. US homebuilders in 2005: roughly 6 to 8x peak earnings, after which earnings went negative and the stocks fell 70% and more. Dry bulk shipping in 2007: low multiples on peak charter rates, then declines of 90% and more.

The common thread is not the multiple. It is that the earnings were spot-priced. When the spot price turned, the denominator vanished, and the low multiple turned out to be the market pricing that evaporation in advance. That base rate is exactly why memory trades at 2x and not 12x today.

Where this cycle differs is confined to the contracted share: multi-year agreements with minimum pricing, and 12.9B dollars of contract liabilities on Micron's balance sheet at fiscal 2026 year end per its 10-K, cash collected in advance. text:
$SPCX - Morgan Stanley works through the economics of a single Starship launch carrying Starlink V3 satellites and concludes that it pays back its variable cost in about 19 weeks of operating profit, less than half the time it estimates for SpaceX's AI compute business. 

It keeps its Overweight rating and $300 price target, more than double the current price per share.

Morgan Stanley puts a full payload at 50 Tbps of gross capacity, of which 2.5 Tbps is salable. 

The step up from the current fleet is large:
- Each V3 satellite has about ten times the downlink capacity of the V2 Mini satellites flown on Falcon 9. 
- One Starship launch adds 20 to 25 times the bandwidth of a Falcon 9 launch, equal to two or three months of Falcon 9 Starlink flights. 
- SpaceX stopped flying Starlink missions on Falcon 9 from Florida in late August, leaving Vandenberg as its only Falcon 9 Starlink pad. 

Morgan Stanley also expects Starship to cut SpaceX's internal variable launch cost from about $1,000 per kilogram in 2026 to about $500 by 2030 and about $140 by 2040, and expects weekly Starship launches by the end of 2027. It notes that Starlink V4 is planned at roughly ten times the capacity of V3 again.

At about $140 the stock is 4% above its $135 offer price, while Morgan Stanley's 2027 and 2028 EPS estimates have risen 80% and 60% since early July.

en_summary: $ES_f Speculation about the SPX path. We’re so accustomed to BTFD and V-shaped recoveries that no one wants to miss the chance to be celebrated for picking the bottom. A gap higher (1.50-2.5%) on Monday would likely correct the oversold reading, but it would be negative.
